note: Drafted posts for the "Just Ship It. It'll be Fine." series. `body` is hand-written or model-drafted from a queue candidate; `status` is owned by a human and is never changed by a harvest. Statuses: draft -> approved -> published. `publishOrder` is the intended sequence, which is NOT the series number: the intro goes out second and gets pinned, because an intro has to earn attention on its own and the takeover post does that better. FORMATTING: one idea per line-group, blank line between. It reads far better on a phone, which is where this is read.

posts.title: Agentic team means at least four different things
posts.body:
"Agentic team" means at least four quite different things, and most of the time two people are describing different ones to each other and agreeing.

A swarm — AI helpers created to do one job, working side by side, gone when it's finished. This is the version most engineers mean, and it genuinely works.

Role-play — a Researcher, a Writer, a Critic. Usually one AI wearing different hats, all sharing exactly the same access to everything. The job titles are instructions, not restrictions.

A fleet — permanent assistants living inside a big platform you already pay for. They work because the platform was already there and had already decided who is allowed to see what.

Or a workflow — ordinary software doing most of the work by following rules, with AI only where something genuinely needs judgement.

Four quite different machines, one phrase, and almost nothing in common between them.

What separates them isn't how many there are or how clever any one of them is. It's whether any of them can be stopped by something other than being asked nicely.

So: ask which of the four you are being sold, and ask them to say it in those terms.

It is not a gotcha. A good vendor will answer it in a sentence and be pleased you asked. In my experience the question produces a much longer pause than it should — and the length of that pause is most of what you needed to know.

posts.title: Six questions for anyone selling you an agentic team
posts.body:
If somebody is selling you an "agentic team" and you don't build software, you are not going to out-argue them on the technology.

Nor do you need to.

But there are a few things worth knowing before you walk into the conversation.

Mostly, you need to be specific about your why — what are you actually trying to achieve? We'll look at that properly in a later post.

And once you're clear on that, you need them to be specific too. These six questions do that. The words in quotes are the ones you'll hear from them.

1. How much of this is a "model", and how much is plain software following a rule?

The model is the AI itself — the part that reads and writes. It costs money every time it runs, and it can answer differently tomorrow from the same starting point. Plain software does the same thing every time and can be explained afterwards. Most of what a business needs done in a week wants the second one. "It's all AI" is an answer, and an expensive one.

2. Can an "agent" act, or only propose?

An agent is a model given tools — the ability to actually do something, send the email, raise the invoice, rather than just write words. That is the whole meaning of the word. It is the difference between a new starter who emails your client directly and one who leaves it in your drafts. If the answer is "we've prompted it not to" — a prompt being the instructions it's given — then it can. It has been asked not to.

3. What are the "guardrails", exactly?

Ask what kind of thing the safety net is. If it's another model checking the first model, it can be talked round the same way the first one was. A limit that is built into the software is a different kind of thing entirely.

4. Where does the work live between being asked for and being done?

If the answer is "in the context window" — the AI's short-term memory, which doesn't survive being closed — ask what happens when you approve something tomorrow morning rather than now. Real work waits overnight. Demos never have to.

5. What does the "integration" actually hand over?

Connecting your accounting system usually means giving them a key — a token — that keeps working long after the meeting. Ask where it's kept, who can see it, and how you cancel it without ringing anyone. It is the largest risk in the arrangement and almost never on the slide.

6. Is the approval structural, or behavioural?

Meaning: is it stopped by the way the software is built, or by the AI having been told to stop? That's question two again, asked at the end on purpose, because the first answer is usually the optimistic one.

None of these require you to understand how any of it works. They require the seller to be specific, which is the actual test.

I'd apply all six to us as well. That's rather the point of writing them down.

posts.title: Half our work has no model in it, deliberately
posts.body:
Everyone is putting AI into everything. About half of what we run has no model in it at all — no AI in the path — on purpose. I'd say that number should be higher in most of what I get shown.

We keep a list of roughly a hundred and forty jobs a business does over and over. Chase an overdue account. Follow up a quote. Tell a subcontractor his insurance runs out in a fortnight.

Going through them honestly, about half are mechanical. Not simple — mechanical. Something crosses a line, we check it against the system that actually holds the record, we write it from a template, we apply the owner's rules about what needs his say-so, and it goes.

Chasing a sixty-three-day invoice is a comparison, a check and a template.

Put a model in the middle of that and you buy three things: a cost every time it runs, a delay, and the possibility of a different answer tomorrow from the same starting point. What you lose is the thing that matters most — when the owner asks why it sent that, there's a reason he can read.

About one job in seven genuinely needs judgement. A quote for something unusual. A "can you sharpen the price" conversation. An argument about scope halfway through. Those want a model, and they'll take most of the work to build, which is a neat illustration of how badly effort and volume line up.

So the first question isn't about the AI. It's which half is which — and whether anyone has been made to defend where they drew the line.

posts.title: Ask your agentic team vendor for a story like this. Then listen to how they tell it.
posts.body:
Ask your agentic team vendor for a story like this one.

Then listen to how they tell it, because that is the part that tells you who you are dealing with.

Here is mine, from last week.

"Nothing that thinks is allowed to send anything." We had that principle written down and logged properly, and I'd have told you we had it.

The client tells the agent what they want to happen — email this quote to this client — and that goes onto a waiting list, an outbox. A second, much stupider piece of software picks it up and carries it out, but only after the approval has landed. The whole point of the stupid one is that it has no judgement in it. There is nothing there to talk round.

What I found is that the stupid one only knew how to do a single kind of job. Send an email.

Our own database has a column that says what kind of job each one is. The note beside it, written by us months ago, lists the examples: raise an invoice, book an appointment. Neither had been built yet. The day either was, the owner would have approved it, it would have gone onto the list, and then it would have sat there.

No error. Nothing retried. Nothing red on any screen. Waiting, in a system reporting itself in perfect health.

And the owner would have had no way of knowing. He approved it. He'd have assumed it went.

Four things to listen for when your vendor tells you theirs.

Did they find it, or did a customer? Everybody has failures. Only some of them are looking.

How did they find it? Mine is dull: I was writing an honest inventory of what the system can actually do, and the sentence I was typing said any kind of job while the code said one. A specific answer is a real answer. "Our monitoring picked it up" invites the obvious follow-up — what alerted, and who read it?

What would it have looked like from your side? If they say "nothing at all, and that is exactly the problem", they have met the expensive kind of failure. A vendor who only has stories about things that threw an error has not.

How did they prove the fix works? I renamed the single entry on that list and watched three of its checks go red, then put it back and watched them go green. A check you have never once seen fail is not a check, and that goes for theirs too.

If they have no story at all, that is also an answer. Either it is very new, or nobody has gone looking.

posts.title: Do not ask which approach is right. Ask why they chose theirs.
posts.body:
A very reasonable question, put to me directly this week: surely you set up a team of specialists in advance — one that knows how you write quotes, one that knows your contacts, one that writes the letter — and the system hands work to whichever one fits.

It is the picture nearly everyone has, and you will see it on a slide. I have argued the other way, and I want to put the argument and my doubt about it in the same place, because you are going to have to judge somebody else's version of this.

The argument is that what you want ready in advance is not a set of assistants sitting there waiting. It is the instructions: what this one is for, what it is allowed to see, what it is allowed to propose — written down and agreed before any work turns up. That gives you everything "prepared" is meant to give, with nothing actually running.

And most of what people want a permanent assistant for turns out, on inspection, to be a permanent fact. Not something that reads the owner's last twenty quotes every single time, but the shape of how he writes a quote, worked out once and written down.

The doubt is that this is extremely convenient for someone whose setup has nowhere to put a permanently running assistant anyway. I cannot fully separate my reasoning from my own constraints, and I would rather say so than pretend.

So do not ask a vendor which approach is right. Ask why they chose theirs — and whether they would still choose it if their setup allowed the other.

Somebody who can answer that has thought about it. Somebody who tells you their way is simply how it is done has not, and you will be paying for that either way.

posts.title: Write down the ten jobs that eat your Tuesday. Then hand the list over.
posts.body:
A hundred and forty jobs on our list, sorted by how they actually have to get done:

About half are mechanical. Something crosses a line, we check it against the system that holds the record, we write it from a template, we apply the owner's rules, it goes. No AI anywhere in it.

About a quarter are a conversation.

About one in seven genuinely needs judgement — and that seventh will take most of the work to build.

The rest sit in between: the system gets everything ready, a person decides.

Those last two lines are the useful ones. Effort and volume come apart badly here, and it explains something I kept noticing in demos and couldn't put my finger on. The clever seventh is the impressive part, so it is the part that gets shown — and it is a thin slice of what a business actually needs done in a week.

Here is how to use that in the room.

Write down the ten jobs you actually want taken off your desk. Not the exciting ones. The ten that eat Tuesday.

Hand the list over and ask them to sort it: which of these need judgement, and which are just rules being followed?

If everything on your list comes back as the clever kind, they have priced the demo rather than your week. If most of it comes back as rules, ask what the AI is doing in the price.

The unimpressive half is where your value is. It wants to be explainable far more than it wants to be clever.

posts.title: For fifteen days, our payment path would hand a customer account to anyone who asked.
posts.body:
For fifteen days, our payment path would hand a paying customer's account to anyone who asked for it.

I was walking that path for the first time — and only to check the wording on a button. The path itself was done. Built, reviewed, shipped, working.

If you'd asked me, I'd have told you so. Confidently.

Here's what I found instead.

Started a checkout. Typed someone else's email into the payment form.

Completed it (to note, we bill in arrears, so nothing is actually due that day, on your own card).

Took the session id out of the address bar. Then set a random password I liked.

Their account was then mine. And everything in it.

This is Kira, whose entire proposition is that a business owner tells her the things he hasn't told his staff or his family. It is the worst defect this codebase can carry, and it was live for fifteen days.

And yet nothing about it looks like an attack.

It's a completed purchase, a real payment, a working signup — right up until it's his account on somebody else's screen.

The obvious fix is to validate the email.

But you can't.

The payment form lets anyone type any address, and it has to — people pay for things on behalf of other people every day. That endpoint cannot obtain proof of who paid.

So the answer isn't better checking. It's refusing to change anything at all for an identity you can't prove.

An existing account now has nothing touched. Not the password, not their valuation, not their subscription.

They're sent to sign in, where forgotten-password proves ownership by email — the proof we can't fake.

I confirmed it by running the attack against our own account, before and after. Then reverted the fix to watch the test go red again.

That part we're good at. Find it, define it, fix it, wire the fix into the regime so it can't come back.

But here's the part that actually keeps me up.

I didn't find this one with a test. Or a scanner. Or a review. I found it because I was checking the wording on a button.

Closing this one took an afternoon. Finding it took an accident.

Finding (or imagining) edge cases to test is a real skill — and I admit, we're still working on how we automate that.

So — where's the path through your product that nobody has yet had a reason to walk?

posts.title: This one's clean. Ship it.
posts.footerOverride:
Just Ship It. It'll be Fine.
What we were sure of, what happened next, and what we changed so it can't go the same way twice. Monthly-ish.
posts.body:
This one's clean. Ship it.

I've said that sentence a lot.

Usually on a Tuesday, usually with someone waiting, and usually with good reason — tests green, review done, everything I know how to check, checked.

The feedback tends to arrive within the hour.

I build AI products more or less on my own. A portfolio of them, sharing one set of foundations, so each new one costs less to ship than the last.

Which means I get to make the same category of mistake across a lot of surfaces, quite fast.

After about the fourth one I started writing them down instead of just wincing.

They have a shape, and the confidence is always real — that's what makes them worth writing about.

Every check we ran was correct. Every one of them answered its question honestly.

The question just turned out not to be the one that mattered.

The site responded, so we thought it was live. It was serving a build from a month earlier.

The page returned 200, so we thought it was fine. Nobody without an account could open it.

The widget rendered, so we thought it worked. It swallowed every question typed into it and never once called the server.

That last kind is getting more common, and it's the reason I'm bothering to write any of this down.

When you ship a page, broken looks broken.

When you ship an agent, broken looks fluent.

One of ours told a customer she couldn't do something she was perfectly capable of — and then filed her own excuse away as a fact about him.

Every part of that exchange looked healthy.

So: a few of these a month. What we were sure of, what happened next, and what's changed so it can't go the same way twice.

That's a deliberately narrow promise. It will go a different way. It keeps doing that.

The most I've managed is to turn each one into something structural — a check that runs whether or not I remember it, a standard written down where the next person will hit it — so the specific humiliation doesn't repeat.

None of them are hypothetical.

All of them were green.

posts.title: She told the customer she couldn't. She could.
posts.body:
She told the customer she couldn't. She could.

An owner said Kira couldn't reach his documents.

I didn't believe him. I'd wired that myself, tested it, watched it work.

I spent longer than I'd like defending the software to the person using it.

He was right.

Kira reads a business owner's files, contacts and mail on his own account, with his permission. The access was live.

She simply told him it wasn't.

And she did it fluently — no error, no hedging, a calm and confident account of a limitation that did not exist.

Then it got worse in a way I hadn't considered.

That exchange went into her memory, and she'd distilled it into a fact about him. Filed under his business, as though the missing capability were a feature of his situation rather than a mistake of hers.

The wrong answer was now durable. And it would shape the next one.

The obvious fix is to test that the tools work.

We had. They did — every tool answered every direct call correctly.

What we'd never tested is whether she believed she had them. And an agent's belief about its own capabilities is not something any integration test touches.

She now has to record why she declined, as a separate act. "She refused" and "she never had the capability" used to look identical from outside.

And her own excuses are no longer eligible to become facts about a customer.

Still open, honestly — she logs it more often than she used to. Not always.

The bit I keep chewing on isn't that she got it wrong.

It's that her mistake became a fact about him.

What stops your system learning from its own errors?

posts.title: She remembered everything. She couldn't recall a word of it.
posts.body:
She remembered everything. She couldn't recall a word of it.

The memory loop was the part I was most confident about.

It's what Kira is — an owner explains how his business actually works, over months, and she holds it.

Built, tested, and published as a shared package for the other products to use.

Then someone came back for a second conversation and she didn't know him.

Not vaguely. She knew a conversation had happened — the flag saying "this person has history" was true and correct.

She just couldn't produce a single thing from it.

The recall query filtered on the agent's id matching the agent's id. Which sounds tautological, and is — except that the path we'd documented and recommended leaves that field empty.

And empty isn't equal to anything. Including itself.

So every fact she had chosen to keep was excluded from the one query that needed it.

Nothing errored. Nothing was wrong.

And yet she couldn't tell him one thing he'd told her.

The obvious fix is to check that memory is being written.

We had. It was — rows present, correct, growing steadily.

Storage was perfect and recall was zero. From the outside, those two are the same picture.

The probe we run now doesn't ask whether history exists. It asks her to say something from it, and fails if she can't.

What's your test that memory works, as opposed to storage?

I thought I had one.

posts.title: We gave her one new tool. It quietly took away all the others.
posts.body:
We gave her one new tool. It quietly took away all the others.

Completely routine — adding a single capability to an agent that already had a dozen.

Deployed it, moved on, thought about it no further.

A week or so later I noticed she'd stopped doing something she used to do well: handing a long job to the background worker instead of sitting on it.

Nothing had touched that code.

The call that attaches a tool doesn't add one. It replaces the entire list.

It's named like an add and behaves like a set — so every re-provision since had been shipping whatever list happened to be sitting in one script.

Its sibling is worse.

An agent came out of provisioning with no tools at all, while the log recorded success.

An agent with no tools looks completely normal. She talks, she's pleasant, she's contextually sharp.

She simply cannot do anything. And she doesn't mention it.

The obvious fix is to remember that the list is a replacement.

That's a rule. And a rule holds right up until one in the morning with someone waiting.

The list is single-sourced with the prompt now, and provisioning reads back what it made. An agent with an empty tool list is a failure, not a success with nothing in it.

A week is a long time not to notice.

If a capability quietly dropped off yours tonight, what would catch it?

Genuinely asking. Everything I had said it was fine.

posts.title: I checked it six times. It worked four.
posts.body:
I checked it six times. It worked four.

Kira offers you a text box if you haven't got a microphone.

I'd checked it was there. Then I was back in that file later, checked again out of habit, and it wasn't.

So I ran it six times across one afternoon, with no changes in between.

Nothing. Then 40%. Then 50, 70, 80, 100.

My honest first reaction was that I must be testing it wrong. Nobody's first thought is that identical code is behaving differently.

It wasn't me.

The box only appeared once the voice connection had actually errored — and a connection that neither connects nor fails, just sits there, never triggers that.

So the same build handed a working widget to one visitor and a dead one to the next.

And it self-selected beautifully. The people it failed are the ones without a microphone, who don't write in to complain.

They just go.

The obvious fix is to test that the fallback appears.

It does. About a third of the time.

It now falls back on a timer as well as an error. Eight seconds, not two, because firing early would steal a slow-but-working connection from someone who does have a mic.

The fix took an hour.

Trusting a single green run — for years — is the part I'd take back.

What are you testing exactly once?

posts.title: Eight things broken. Four shipped that morning, by someone who checked all four.
posts.body:
Eight things broken. Four shipped that morning, by someone who checked all four.

It had been a good morning.

Every change verified, every check green, every one of them reported honestly.

Nothing skipped. Nobody rushing for the door.

Then a tester walked the product and came back with eight problems. Four of them hours old.

So my first question was: what did we miss?

Because on paper, nothing.

What we missed is that all the checking asked "did my change take effect" — and the answer was yes, every time.

Six of the eight weren't in anything that had changed.

They sat at the joins. A header added without noticing the layout already drew one. A price corrected on the checkout page while the page immediately before it still read "+ GST + GST".

We'd fixed the exact thing the report named and left the same thing alive two screens over.

Three separate times in one day.

And yet nobody did anything wrong. Every change was verified, and every verification was honest.

The obvious fix is to check more carefully.

But it was already careful. It was just aimed at the diff.

Verifying your change tells you what you wrote. It tells you nothing about what the customer gets.

So the unit is the whole path someone walks now, including the parts nobody touched. And nothing closes until we've gone looking for the same mistake everywhere else.

I wouldn't call this solved.

We're getting caught out in new places rather than the same ones. Which is progress, and isn't the same thing.

posts.title: Four checks reported numbers they hadn't earned. Three were in the tool built to catch that.
posts.body:
Four checks reported numbers they hadn't earned. Three of them were in the tool I built to catch exactly that.

I spent an afternoon writing a harvester.

It reads the places we write lessons down, and finds the ones that never reached the knowledge base. Deterministic, self-tested, no model in the loop.

I was quite pleased with it.

Then I backfilled twelve entries covering twelve gaps it had itself named, re-ran it, and the count went from 50 to 49.

The backfill was fine.

The measurement had a length bias — it divided shared words by the candidate's word count, so a long document could never score as covered, no matter how thoroughly it was recorded.

It would have reported those as outstanding forever. And a number that only ever rises reads as thoroughness.

Three more turned up the same afternoon.

An analysis that fell back to a title when a field was missing, and produced a confident 0.83 match that meant nothing.

A merge that never refreshed old rows — so a fix never reached the data it was written for, and a missing field got read as "nothing to worry about".

And a self-test printing "14/14 passed" as a hardcoded string. Still printing it after I'd added three more checks.

And yet nothing errored.

Every one of those numbers arrived on time, correctly formatted, from a tool with a passing test suite.

The obvious fix is to test the tool.

It had eighteen tests. They all passed. Not one of them asked whether the summary line was true.

The count is counted now rather than written down. And every threshold gets checked in both directions — a check that can only ever say "gap" is not a check.

I only found them because I happened to doubt a number I had no particular reason to doubt.

How do you go looking for the checks that are lying?

posts.title: Eight words you'll hear in an agentic pitch, and what each one costs you
posts.body:
Eight words you'll hear in any "agentic" pitch, what each one actually means, and what it changes about what you're buying.

Model. The AI itself — the part that reads and writes. You pay each time it runs, and it can give a different answer tomorrow from the same starting point. That's fine for judgement and wrong for anything that has to be identical every time.

Prompt. The instructions the model is given. Worth knowing because "we've prompted it not to" is a request, not a restriction. It describes what they've asked for, not what the thing can do.

Agent. A model that's been given tools — the ability to act, not just write. This is the word doing the most work in the whole pitch, and the one to slow down on.

Tools. What it's allowed to reach: your email, your accounting system, your calendar. Ask for the list. "It has access to your systems" is not a list.

Orchestration. Deciding which part does what, in what order. Ask whether that decision is itself made by AI, or by ordinary software. Both are legitimate; only one is predictable.

Guardrails. Whatever stops it doing something daft. Ask what kind of thing they are. AI checking AI can be talked round; a limit built into the software cannot.

Context window. The AI's short-term memory for one conversation. It does not survive being closed, so if the work lives there, it doesn't survive an approval that lands tomorrow.

Token. In this setting, the key that lets them into your systems, which usually keeps working long after the meeting. Ask how you cancel it.

None of this makes you an expert, and it isn't meant to. It makes you hard to bluff, which is a different and more useful thing.
